items.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
items.summary: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

items.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. 

  • CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Summary

ROS# before version 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that could allow an attacker that is able to pass a crafted message definition file to the user to inject arbitrary code into the generated program. Siemens has released a new version for ROS# and recommends to update to the latest version.

The following versions of Siemens ROS# are affected:

  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

Affected systems do not properly escape text of message definition files. This could allow an attacker that is able to pass a crafted message definition file to the user to inject arbitrary code into the generated program.

Acknowledgments

  • Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

items.title: Dorsett Controls InfoScan
items.summary:
View CSAF

Summary

Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to retrieve sensitive system information, access application data without authorization, recover stored credentials, or intercept and manipulate network communications.

The following versions of Dorsett Controls InfoScan are affected:

  • InfoScan <=1.45.0 (CVE-2026-117659, CVE-2026-120157, CVE-2026-120255, CVE-2026-120260, CVE-2026-120271, CVE-2026-120298)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 8.1 Dorsett Controls InfoScan
5 Vulnerabilities
Improper Certificate Validation, Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere, Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: United States

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-117659
The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection.
Read More

1 Affected Product

Dorsett Controls InfoScan <=1.45.0

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Dorsett Controls recommends updating affected versions of InfoScan to v1.46 or higher. To install the security patch, user administrators will need to log in to InfoScan and select System Maintenance from the menu. Once the System Maintenance application is open, select Check for Updates, and click the Install Now button in the Ready To Install section. If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the update from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal.

items.summary:
View CSAF

Summary

Mendix Studio Pro contains multiple vulnerabilities in the MCP Server, that could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the server remotely or trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests, potentially leading to unauthorized data access, tool execution, or system compromise. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.

The following versions of Siemens Mendix Studio Pro are affected:

  • Mendix Studio Pro 11 vers:intdot/>=11.15.0|<11.16.0 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137)
  • Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 vers:intdot/>=11.12.6|<11.12.7 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 8.8 Siemens Mendix Studio Pro 11
2 Vulnerabilities
Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-112136
The affected products MCP Server does not properly restrict its HTTP listener to the loopback interface, leaving it potentially exposed to remote systems. This could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the MCP Server remotely.
Read More

2 Affected Products

Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Mitigation
Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.

Vendor fix
Update to V11.16.0 or later version

Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 >= V11.12.6 < V11.12.7

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Mitigation
Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.

Vendor fix
Update to V11.12.7 or later version

The affected products MCP Server does not properly validate Content-Type and Origin headers on incoming HTTP requests, leaving it vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). This could allow a malicious web page to trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests and executing unintended actions on the local MCP Server.

Utilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1).

items.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
items.summary:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

  • Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.
  • Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
    • If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.
  • Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.
  •  Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

Resources

CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:

Vendor Guidance

  • Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Update – November 2026

The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Please also have a look on following Software Field Bulletins: Teamcenter: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869204 Polarion: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869197 Manufacturing Operations Center (Opcenter) and Process Preparation X: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869211 Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Automation Software Products are affected:

  • COMOS Walkinside vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • gDAP (gPROMS Digital Application Platform) vers:all/* ()
  • Project Server Web Administration Tool vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC BRAUMAT vers:intdot/>=8.2.0.1|<8.2.0.5 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC Profiling Tool vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC SISTAR vers:intdot/>=8.2.0.1|<8.2.0.5 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Companion vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC OA V3.20 vers:intdot/<3.20.17.1 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC OA V3.21 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Unified for Industrial Edge vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • SIMATIC WinCC Unified PC Runtime vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)

  • SIMATIC WinCC V7/V8 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)

  • User Management Component (UMC) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 9.8 Siemens COMOS Walkinside
1 Vulnerability
Out-of-bounds Write

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Food and Agriculture, Energy
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-111497
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.
Read More

Temporarily disable Brotli compression and decompression at the application or proxy layer if it is not strictly required

items.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
items.summary:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Background

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-109618
PHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).
Read More

1 Affected Product

RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS (10.2 All, 11.1 All, 11.2 All, 12.1 All, 12.2 All)

Product Status: known_affected

Vendor fix
Upgrade to corresponding available PAN-OS version. Contact customer support to receive additional patch and update information.

Relevant CWE: CWE-416 Use After Free

CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String

CVE-2026-109619
PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE).

items.title: Siemens Desigo, Gridscale
items.summary:
View CSAF

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.

The following versions of Siemens Desigo, Gridscale are affected:

  • Desigo CC family V8 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • Desigo CC family V9 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • Gridscale X DSA vers:intdot/>=5.3|<5.4 (CVE-2026-111497)

  • Gridscale X PSS®E vers:intdot/<36.8.0 (CVE-2026-111497)

     

CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 9.8 Siemens Desigo CC family V8
1 Vulnerability
Out-of-bounds Write

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information Technology
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-111497
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.
Read More

4 Affected Products

Desigo CC family V8

Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Install the latest .NET security updates via Windows Update.

Desigo CC family V9

Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Install the latest .NET security updates via Windows Update.

Gridscale X DSA >= V5.3 < V5.4

Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Update to V5.4 or later version

Gridscale X PSS®E < V36.8.0

Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Update to V36.8.0 or later version

CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String
3.1 9.8 CRITICAL CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

View CVE Details

Acknowledgments

  • Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.

General Recommendations

Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project and security researchers disclosed two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime known as "php2shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines, and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Siemens is actively monitoring the situation and assessing the implications of these vulnerabilities on our portfolio. Because this evaluation is ongoing, our findings are subject to change as new technical details and vendor updates emerge. We will publish updated findings, guidance, and remediation recommendations as soon as they become available. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

Palo Alto Networks has published information on a vulnerability in PAN-OS related to the Node2Shell vulnerability. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by this vulnerability. Customers are advised to consult and implement the workarounds provided in Palo Alto Networks' upstream security notifications. 

The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 are affected:

  • RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

items.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary:
CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
items.summary:
CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available. 

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts. 

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC. 

Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

items.title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
items.summary:
Overview

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

Threat

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:

  • Authentication bypass;
  • Arbitrary code injection; and
  • Weak configurations.

Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:

  • Change of temperature, which could:
    • Affect the service life of the system;
    • Create a fire hazard;
    • Cause loss of inventory; or
    • Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.
  • Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).

Mitigations

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

  • Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.
  • Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].
  • Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].
  • Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.
  • Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].
  • Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].
  • Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity.
    • For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.
  • Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Resources

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

  • CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology
  • CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security
  • CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance
  • United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT

Contact Information

The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet:

  • Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident:
    • Date, time, and location of the incident;
    • Type of activity;
    • Number of people affected;
    • Type of equipment used for the activity; and
    • Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact.
  • Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.

items.title: LinuxのLinux Kernelにおける不特定の脆弱性
items.summary: Linuxカーネルにおいて、以下の脆弱性が修正されました。KVM: x86のemulator_pio_inから高速INを廃止しました。__emulator_pio_in()がカーネル内でPIOを処理する際に"val"を設定するようになったため、高速PIOではemulator_pio_in()を経由せず、直接__emulator_pio_in()を使用する仕様に変更されました。vcpu-＞arch.pio.countは確実に'0'であるため、これは純粋なnop（何もしない処理）となります。現在、emulator_pio_in_emulatedがemulator_pio_inの最後の呼び出し元となっています。機能的な変更は意図されていません。

items.title: オラクルのOracle One-to-One Fulfillmentにおけるアクセス制御に関する脆弱性
items.summary: Oracle E-Business SuiteのOracle One-to-One Fulfillment製品（コンポーネント：Documents）に存在する脆弱性です。影響を受けるサポート対象バージョンは12.2.3から12.2.15までです。悪用が困難なこの脆弱性により、HTTP経由でネットワークアクセス可能な低権限の攻撃者がOracle One-to-One Fulfillmentを侵害する可能性があります。この脆弱性が成功裏に悪用されると、重要なデータやOracle One-to-One Fulfillmentでアクセス可能な全データに対して不正に作成、削除、または変更する権限が攻撃者に与えられるほか、Oracle One-to-One Fulfillmentをハングさせたり、頻繁に再現可能なクラッシュ（完全なDoS）を引き起こす能力も攻撃者に与える可能性があります。CVSS 3.1 基本スコアは6.8（整合性および可用性への影響）です。CVSSベクター：(CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H)

items.title: オラクルのOracle One-to-One Fulfillmentにおけるアクセス制御に関する脆弱性

items.title: MongoDB Inc.のLibmongocryptにおける整数アンダーフローの脆弱性
items.summary: MongoDBのlibmongocryptのKMSエンドポイント解析ロジックにおける整数のアンダーフローにより、割り当ての失敗が発生し、アプリケーションプロセスが終了する可能性があります。これは、認証されたユーザーがキー保管コレクション内のキー文書を変更した場合、またはアプリケーションがキー作成時にパスやクエリの後にコロンを含むKMSエンドポイントを受け入れた場合に発生する可能性があります。この問題は割り当てられた境界外のメモリにはアクセスしないものです。

items.title: MongoDB Inc.のMondoDB C++ Driverにおける解釈の競合に関する脆弱性
items.summary: MongoDB C++ドライバーは、コレクションAPIで許可される特定のフィールド名およびコレクション名に埋め込まれたNULバイト以降の内容を破棄します。これにより、ドライバーと呼び出し元アプリケーションが同じ名前を異なる方法で解釈する可能性があります。影響を受けるアプリケーションによって渡される名前に影響を与えられる認証済みの攻撃者は、アプリケーションが意図しないフィールドから異なる値を読み取ったり、意図しないコレクションの名前を変更したりする行為を引き起こす可能性があります。これらの操作はアプリケーションの既存のデータベース認証情報を使用して実行されます。

items.title: MongoDB Inc.のMongoDB C Driverにおける境界外書き込みに関する脆弱性

items.title: Java4Shell, NGINX2Shell and more: Why we are not at "Yellow", (Wed, Nov 18th)
items.summary: About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today.

items.summary: CVE-2026-102895 is a trivial authentication-bypass vulnerability. GPUStack is also an attractive target. It is open-source software that manages clusters of GPUs, which are typically used to run AI workloads. All versions of GPUStack prior to 2.2.0, which was released at the end of June. This vulnerability was not made public until the end of July, and the CVE was assigned on November 4th.

items.title: Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports
items.summary:
Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers used codename MDASH to investigate Linux kernel vulnerabilities, resulting in 59 upstream bug reports, 33 assigned CVEs, and 38 merged fixes. The research includes eight demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits and examines the challenges of turning AI-generated findings into validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes.

items.title: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust
items.summary:
Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers found memory-safety bugs in Rust's core and std libraries, including cases where safe Rust code can trigger undefined behavior. Using Hyenas, FORGE's frontier research version of codename MDASH, the team investigated three patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code and what they reveal about Rust's safety guarantees.

The post FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.

items.title: CVE-2026-123007: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Integer Underflow Leads to RCE (FIXED)
items.summary:
Overview

Today, both Rapid7 and F5 are disclosing CVE-2026-123007, a critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2, which can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against affected servers under certain conditions.

CVE ID

Description

CWE

CVSSv4

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption permitting worker-context RCE

CWE-191 (Integer Underflow)

9.2 (Critical)

nginx can miscalculate how much response data an HTTP/2 client has allowed it to send. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this error by cancelling queued response data, then make nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response. The resulting memory corruption can disclose data, interrupt service, and execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Impact

Rapid7 has developed a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated RCE against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8, as shown below in Figure 1. The target nginx server’s configuration had http2 on and TLS enabled. Note that for brevity, video playback is at 8x speed.

Figure 1: Video demonstrating unauthenticated RCE against NGINX 1.31.8 via CVE-2026-123007

Leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for RCE requires a significant amount of network traffic to be transmitted, approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data. Both available network bandwidth and connection timeouts will place practical limitations on Internet exploitation. In the above example shown in Figure 1, exploitation takes two and a half minutes. The approximate timings to transmit the required network data over a 10 Gbit/s network is two minutes, while on a 1 Gbit/s network it is seventeen minutes. Due to nginx’s default one hour connection lifetime, a network slower than approximately 300 Mbit/s will take over the one hour connection limit threshold and will not be able to succeed. Additionally, should an HTTP/2 connection be proxied, the precise attacker-controlled HTTP/2 frames being transmitted will likely not be retransmitted in a way that satisfies exploiting the vulnerability.

Finally, the exploitation strategy developed depends on a specific x86-64 glibc EVEX/YMM memcpy implementation selected at runtime, based on the avx512f and avx512vl CPU features. Alternative RCE exploitation strategies may be viable, but none are currently known.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Stephen Fewer, Senior Principal Security Researcher at Rapid7, and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

Technical analysis

The version of nginx tested was a linux/amd64 Docker image for nginx version 1.31.8 (nginx@sha256:5ab5b0b01097420873a3f3330f44248e34a3c2a3e8d5ee30658aeae8cb7435da), and ran with an exposed HTTPS service and http2 enabled.

How a client controls HTTP/2 response data

HTTP/2 carries messages called frames over a connection. Each request and response belongs to a numbered stream, so one connection can carry several exchanges at once. Response-body bytes are carried in DATA frames.

For this vulnerability, nginx is the sender and the remote client is the receiver. The client grants nginx permission, or flow-control credit, to send a certain number of DATA bytes. nginx tracks the remaining credit in two counters: one for each stream and one shared by the connection. Sending DATA must be permitted by both counters. These HTTP/2 counters are separate from TCP's receive window.

The client grants more credit by sending a WINDOW_UPDATE frame containing a positive increment. A stream identifier of zero increases the connection’s send credit. A nonzero stream identifier increases the send credit for the stream with that specific nonzero identifier. HTTP/2 limits the increment and the resulting window to 2^31-1 bytes, or 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF). This report calls that maximum MAX.

The client can also send a SETTINGS frame containing a SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE parameter. This changes the starting credit for new streams. nginx must also adjust each active stream's remaining credit by the difference between the old and new setting values. It does not change the connection's credit. A reduction can therefore leave an active stream with negative credit until the client grants more. The connection window has no equivalent reduction: it must remain between zero and MAX. RFC 9113, section 6.9 defines these limits and the required errors.

nginx stores the connection counter in h2c->send_window, where h2c is the HTTP/2 connection record. Its size_t type is an unsigned integer: on the verified 64-bit build it can hold values from zero to 2^64-1. The size_t type can therefore hold values above HTTP/2's maximum connection window of 2^31-1 bytes (MAX). nginx must enforce that protocol limit in its own logic.

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.h
#define NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW ((1U << 31) - 1) // <--- [1]
struct ngx_http_v2_connection_s {
    // ...
    size_t send_window;                         // <--- [2]
    // ...
};
struct ngx_http_v2_stream_s {
    // ...
    ssize_t send_window;
    // ...
};

The rule that the connection counter at [2] must never exceed MAX at [1] is the connection-window invariant. The separate stream counter, stream->send_window, is explicitly declared as ssize_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. That allows SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE to make a stream's credit temporarily negative. The connection counter remains unsigned. The later unsafe conversion occurs when the output filter treats excessive connection credit as a signed 64-bit off_t response length.

Leveraging vulnerability has four main stages:

  1. By slowing its reading of server output, the client keeps selected DATA frames queued and unstarted. It raises the connection's credit to MAX and the selected streams' credit to just below MAX. A SETTINGS frame that increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough to exceed the stream limit makes nginx close those streams while leaving the connection usable. Request cleanup then restores the reserved credit above MAX.

  2. An unsigned subtraction in the next connection WINDOW_UPDATE check underflows. Repeated accepted WINDOW_UPDATE frames can then raise the counter into the upper half of its 64-bit range without requiring the addition to wrap.

  3. On the verified 64-bit build, nginx interprets that excessive counter as a negative response length and creates an invalid buffer. Buffered TLS output then passes a huge unsigned byte count to the memory-copy function memcpy, causing out-of-bounds reads and writes.

  4. These constrained memory accesses depend on the build and selected copy routine. With a suitable memory layout, an attacker can use disclosed addresses and controlled overwrites to execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Cancelling queued DATA restores too much credit

When nginx queues a DATA frame at [3], it subtracts the frame's DATA length from the connection's credit counter at [4] and then from the stream's credit counter. This reserves the credit before the bytes reach the client and prevents other streams from spending the same connection credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
ngx_http_v2_queue_frame(h2c, frame);       // <--- [3]

h2c->send_window -= frame_size;            // <--- [4]
stream->send_window -= frame_size;
stream->queued++;

An attacker can keep a later response queued by slowing or stopping its reading of earlier server output. Once the transport cannot accept more output, nginx must wait. This condition is transport backpressure. The attacker needs enough of it to keep the selected DATA frame unstarted: none of that frame's bytes have yet entered TLS output or the socket. Stopping response reads does not prevent the client from sending control frames in the other direction.

While the DATA remains queued, the client sends a connection WINDOW_UPDATE that raises nginx's reduced counter to MAX. The problem appears when the request that owns the queued DATA then closes. Its request-cleanup handler removes the unstarted DATA and returns the reserved credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup()
// ...
for ( ;; ) {
    frame = *fn;
    if (frame == NULL) {
        break;
    }
    if (frame->stream == stream && !frame->blocked) { // <--- [5]
        *fn = frame->next;
        window += frame->length;                      // <--- [6]
        if (--stream->queued == 0) {
            break;
        }
        continue;
    }
    fn = &frame->next;
}
// ...
h2c->send_window += window;                           // <--- [7]

The test at [5] selects removable, unstarted frames for that request. The local variable window totals their DATA lengths at [6]. The addition at [7] does not check whether restoring those bytes takes the connection counter above MAX.

For example, restoring 1,393 bytes after the counter has reached 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF) produces 2,147,485,040 (0x80000570). This value is invalid under HTTP/2 as it exceeds MAX, although it still fits in a 64-bit size_t; the addition has not yet wrapped around. The unchecked restoration at [7] is the first invalid state in the vulnerability. The attacker still needs a way to close the selected requests while preserving the connection, so the excessive counter can be used again.

A SETTINGS error closes the stream but leaves the connection usable

When a SETTINGS frame increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough that an active stream's credit would exceed MAX, nginx terminates that stream but leaves the HTTP/2 connection usable. A client can create this condition by first sending a stream WINDOW_UPDATE to put the selected stream just below MAX. It then sends a SETTINGS frame that increases the initial stream-window setting. For example, changing the setting from 65,535 to 65,537 adds two bytes to every active stream. A stream already at MAX-1 would become MAX+1, even though the new setting value itself is allowed.

RFC 9113 requires this condition to end the connection with FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR. nginx instead calls ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream() for each affected stream. That function sends RST_STREAM, which ends an individual stream, and causes the request to be cleaned up. The loop then continues using the same connection:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c
// ngx_http_v2_adjust_windows()
// ...
if (delta > 0
    && stream->send_window
          > (ssize_t) (NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - delta))
{
    if (ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream(h2c, stream,
                                     NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR)
        == NGX_ERROR)
    {
        return NGX_ERROR;
    }
    continue;                                      // <--- [8]
}

Here, delta is the difference between the new and old setting values. Request cleanup performs [5] through [7], while continue at [8] leaves the HTTP/2 connection open. The attacker can now send further frames on the connection whose credit has exceeded MAX.

The next WINDOW_UPDATE causes an integer underflow

When another connection WINDOW_UPDATE arrives, nginx tries to calculate how much additional credit is still allowed:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c
// ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()
// ...
if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { // <--- [9]
    // ...
    return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c,
                                        NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR);
}
h2c->send_window += window;                            // <--- [10]

In this function, window is the increment received from the client. The subtraction at [9] is safe only while the stored counter is no greater than MAX. If cleanup has restored R excess bytes, the intended allowance is MAX - (MAX + R), or -R. Unsigned arithmetic cannot represent that negative result. On the verified 64-bit build it wraps to 2^64 - R, a very large positive number. This is the integer underflow identified by CWE-191.

The incorrect allowance lets further client increments pass the check. By sending many increments, each no greater than MAX, the client can raise the counter to 2^63 or above without wrapping the addition itself, shown at [10] above. Such a value has the top bit of its 64-bit representation set. It is still an unsigned value, but it no longer fits in a signed 64-bit integer. That distinction matters when nginx prepares the next response.

This amplification accounts for the large traffic requirement. A connection WINDOW_UPDATE occupies 13 HTTP/2 bytes: a nine-byte frame header and a four-byte payload. The credit granted by that frame is not data actually transmitted. Starting from the small over-credit state described above, reaching 2^63 by maximum-size increments takes about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB. Reaching the near-2^64 values used for the confirmed read/write path takes about 2^33 increments, or 104 GiB. nginx also limits control-frame traffic relative to other received data. The current code-execution reproduction sends about 15 GiB of additional request-header traffic to stay within that limit, bringing its reported plaintext total to about 119.02 GiB. TLS and network overhead increase the actual wire traffic. These figures describe this 64-bit amplification route, not a universal minimum for every possible exploit.

Excessive credit becomes a negative response length

The client can make an active stream with available credit process an ordinary response body. nginx's HTTP/2 output filter decides how many body bytes to include in a DATA frame. Before following that calculation, it is useful to define the buffer it will create.

An in-memory nginx buffer is described by a ngx_buf_t record. Its pos pointer is the memory address of the next byte to send. Its last pointer is the address immediately after the available data. For four available bytes, last must be four bytes after pos; subtracting pos from last gives the length, four. A valid buffer therefore cannot have last before pos. nginx links these buffer records together into an output chain, which is a list of data waiting to be sent.

In ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), the byte limit is an off_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. The excessive unsigned connection counter is converted to that signed type at [11]. On this build, a value of 2^64 - d, where d is a small positive byte count, becomes -d:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) {
    limit = h2c->send_window;                         // <--- [11]
}
if (limit > stream->send_window) {
    limit = (stream->send_window > 0) ? stream->send_window : 0;
}
// ...
if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) {
    frame_size = (size_t) limit;                      // <--- [12]
}
// ...
rest = frame_size;
while ((off_t) rest >= size) {                        // <--- [13]
    // ...
}
if (rest) {
    cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf,
                                       offset, rest); // <--- [14]
    // ...
}

The stream-window check does not reject a negative limit: it only reduces a limit that is too large. At [12], the negative limit becomes a huge unsigned frame_size. Casting the same value back to off_t makes it negative again, so [13] skips the loop that would normally consume and bound the available body bytes. At [14], nginx passes the invalid length to a helper whose size parameter is also a signed off_t.

That helper creates a shadow buffer: a new metadata record referring to part of the existing response data, without copying the response body itself. It sets the new end pointer using the supplied length:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow()
static ngx_chain_t *
ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(ngx_http_v2_stream_t *stream, ngx_buf_t *buf,
    off_t offset, off_t size)
{
    // ...
    ngx_memcpy(chunk, buf, sizeof(ngx_buf_t));
    // ...
    if (ngx_buf_in_memory(chunk)) {
        chunk->pos += offset;
        chunk->last = chunk->pos + size;              // <--- [15]
    }
    // ...
}

Because size is negative, [15] places last before pos. The response body has not become larger; its buffer metadata is now invalid. The next output stage trusts that metadata.

Buffered TLS output copies beyond the buffers

For buffered TLS output, ngx_ssl_send_chain() gathers bytes from the output chain into a temporary staging buffer before encryption. It calculates each input buffer's length using last - pos. The invalid buffer produces a negative signed length at [16]:

// src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c
// ngx_ssl_send_chain()
// ...
ssize_t send, size, file_size;
// ...
size = in->buf->last - in->buf->pos;                  // <--- [16]
if (size > buf->end - buf->last) {
    size = buf->end - buf->last;
}
if (send + size > limit) {
    size = (ssize_t) (limit - send);
}
// ...
ngx_memcpy(buf->last, in->buf->pos, size);            // <--- [17]
buf->last += size;
in->buf->pos += size;

Both checks only reduce lengths that are too large. Neither rejects a negative length. memcpy takes an unsigned size_t byte count, so [17] converts -d back into the huge value 2^64-d. The actual source and destination buffers are far smaller. This is where the invalid connection credit first reaches an out-of-bounds native memory access.

A copy that actually traversed such an enormous range would normally encounter inaccessible memory and crash the worker. In the tested x86-64 glibc implementation, however, certain lengths just below 2^64 cause the machine-level end-address calculations to wrap (Please see Addendum A below for more details on this unexpected behavior). For a length of 2^64-d, adding the length to a start address can produce an address d bytes before it. The optimized copy uses these end addresses in its loop conditions, so it can finish after a limited number of reads and writes that reach outside the intended buffers. The copy can return if all locations it actually accesses are accessible; other lengths, memory layouts, or copy implementations can fault immediately. If it returns, nginx also moves both buffer positions backward by the negative signed length.

Exploitation

The invalid copy can both read and overwrite worker memory. It does not give the client an HTTP/2 field in which it can simply choose any memory address. The useful addresses depend on where nginx allocated the response and TLS buffers, how much output is already buffered, and which copy routine the C library selected. These are constrained read and write capabilities, not an unconditional arbitrary read or write.

After creating the invalid DATA buffer, ngx_http_v2_send_chain() updates its position in the original response and records the bytes that remain to be sent:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
offset += rest;                                       // <--- [18]
size -= rest;
// ...
if (offset) {
    cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf,
                                       offset, size); // <--- [19]
    // ...
    in->buf = cl->buf;
    // ...
}

Here, offset is the position within the original body and size is its remaining length. Starting at offset zero, the same unsigned value representing -d makes [18] move the offset backward by d and increase the remaining length by d on the verified build. The shadow buffer created at [19] therefore has a positive length, but starts d bytes before the original response and ends at its original end. If the oversized copy and connection survive, later ordinary DATA frames can carry those preceding bytes to the client through TLS. They can include pointers into the heap, where nginx dynamically allocates request data, or into loaded libraries. Those pointers disclose addresses that address-space layout randomization (ASLR) would otherwise hide.

On the write side, nginx stores client-supplied request data in heap allocations. With a suitable allocation layout, the oversized copy can pick up those attacker-selected bytes and replace fields in a nearby live heap object. One useful field is a callback: a stored function pointer that nginx intends to call later. An attacker who knows the relevant process addresses and can overwrite that field may redirect normal nginx processing to existing executable code. The overwrite need not contain new machine code. This explains the general route from disclosed addresses and controlled bytes to code execution; it does not claim that every build exposes the same object or callback. Execution has the worker's permissions; execution as the master process or root has not been established.

The proof-of-concept first recovers heap addresses and pointers into nginx and the GNU C Library (glibc) from memory preceding the original response body. It uses those addresses and the overwrite to forge nginx request and response-buffer objects that return selected parts of glibc's loaded image over HTTP/2. The returned ELF metadata is parsed to resolve system() despite ASLR, then a request-pool cleanup callback is redirected to invoke an attacker-chosen command.

Addendum A: Why an oversized memcpy can return

The TLS copy via ngx_memcpy (shown at [17] above) receives a byte count of 2^64-d, where d is a small positive distance. A routine that actually traversed that entire range would normally fault. This addendum explains why one optimized glibc implementation can instead finish after a limited number of out-of-bounds accesses.

glibc chooses among optimized copy routines according to the CPU's capabilities. The tested x86-64 routine uses EVEX/YMM instructions, which can move 32 bytes at a time. In the corresponding glibc 2.41 source, the EVEX wrapper includes a shared memcpy/memmove implementation, and its vector configuration sets VEC_SIZE to 32. A vector is the block of bytes handled by one such instruction.

The following excerpt uses AT&T assembly syntax, in which the source operand comes first. The CPU register %rdi holds the original destination address, called D below; %rsi holds the source address, Q; and %rdx holds the byte count, n. One route enters this backward-copy branch when D and Q are different and the unsigned difference D-Q is smaller than n. This includes the ordinary case where D is above Q and n is close to the unsigned 64-bit maximum.

// glibc 2.41: sysdeps/x86_64/multiarch/memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S
// Function: CPU-selected memcpy implementation, backward-copy branch
    // ...
L(more_8x_vec_backward):
    // ...
    leaq (VEC_SIZE * -4 + -1)(%rdi, %rdx), %rcx // <--- [20]
    // ...
    andq $-(VEC_SIZE), %rcx                     // <--- [21]
    // ...
L(loop_4x_vec_backward):
    // ... load and store four 32-byte vectors
    addq $(VEC_SIZE * -4), %rcx                 // <--- [22]
    cmpq %rcx, %rdi                             // <--- [23]
    jb L(loop_4x_vec_backward)
    // ... store the previously loaded leading and trailing vectors
    VZEROUPPER_RETURN                           // <--- [24]

The full glibc assembly source shows the omitted loads and stores. At [20], leaq calculates an address without reading memory. Its 64-bit result keeps only the low 64 bits. At [21], andq rounds that address down to a 32-byte boundary. Calling the resulting destination address cursor, the calculation is:

cursor = align_down_32((D + n - 129) modulo 2^64)
       = align_down_32(D - d - 129), when n = 2^64-d

Here, align_down_32 means rounding down to the nearest address divisible by 32; it is explanatory notation, not a glibc function. For an ordinary heap address and a small d, the calculated cursor is already below D.

The loop starts by copying one 128-byte block. Instruction [22] then moves the cursor backward by another 128 bytes. The comparison and unsigned jump at [23] repeat the loop only while D < cursor. Because the cursor is already below D, the jump is not taken. The routine writes its remaining leading and trailing vectors, then returns at [24]. It has not copied the enormous requested range: the wrapped address has made the loop stop after a small set of accesses. Those accesses can still read and overwrite memory outside the actual buffers.

Remediation

The following vendor supplied fixes are available.

Fixed Version

None

For the latest remediation information, please see the vendor advisory.

  • November 11, 2026: Rapid7 makes initial outreach to F5.

  • November 12, 2026: F5 confirms outreach and Rapid7 discloses the vulnerability. F5 confirms receipt of the disclosure.
