raw.title: CVE-2026-123007: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Integer Underflow Leads to RCE (FIXED)
raw.summary:
Overview

Today, both Rapid7 and F5 are disclosing CVE-2026-123007, a critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2, which can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against affected servers under certain conditions.

CVE ID

Description

CWE

CVSSv4

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption permitting worker-context RCE

CWE-191 (Integer Underflow)

9.2 (Critical)

nginx can miscalculate how much response data an HTTP/2 client has allowed it to send. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this error by cancelling queued response data, then make nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response. The resulting memory corruption can disclose data, interrupt service, and execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Impact

Rapid7 has developed a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated RCE against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8, as shown below in Figure 1. The target nginx server’s configuration had http2 on and TLS enabled. Note that for brevity, video playback is at 8x speed.

Figure 1: Video demonstrating unauthenticated RCE against NGINX 1.31.8 via CVE-2026-123007

Leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for RCE requires a significant amount of network traffic to be transmitted, approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data. Both available network bandwidth and connection timeouts will place practical limitations on Internet exploitation. In the above example shown in Figure 1, exploitation takes two and a half minutes. The approximate timings to transmit the required network data over a 10 Gbit/s network is two minutes, while on a 1 Gbit/s network it is seventeen minutes. Due to nginx’s default one hour connection lifetime, a network slower than approximately 300 Mbit/s will take over the one hour connection limit threshold and will not be able to succeed. Additionally, should an HTTP/2 connection be proxied, the precise attacker-controlled HTTP/2 frames being transmitted will likely not be retransmitted in a way that satisfies exploiting the vulnerability.

Finally, the exploitation strategy developed depends on a specific x86-64 glibc EVEX/YMM memcpy implementation selected at runtime, based on the avx512f and avx512vl CPU features. Alternative RCE exploitation strategies may be viable, but none are currently known.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Stephen Fewer, Senior Principal Security Researcher at Rapid7, and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

Technical analysis

The version of nginx tested was a linux/amd64 Docker image for nginx version 1.31.8 (nginx@sha256:5ab5b0b01097420873a3f3330f44248e34a3c2a3e8d5ee30658aeae8cb7435da), and ran with an exposed HTTPS service and http2 enabled.

How a client controls HTTP/2 response data

HTTP/2 carries messages called frames over a connection. Each request and response belongs to a numbered stream, so one connection can carry several exchanges at once. Response-body bytes are carried in DATA frames.

For this vulnerability, nginx is the sender and the remote client is the receiver. The client grants nginx permission, or flow-control credit, to send a certain number of DATA bytes. nginx tracks the remaining credit in two counters: one for each stream and one shared by the connection. Sending DATA must be permitted by both counters. These HTTP/2 counters are separate from TCP's receive window.

The client grants more credit by sending a WINDOW_UPDATE frame containing a positive increment. A stream identifier of zero increases the connection’s send credit. A nonzero stream identifier increases the send credit for the stream with that specific nonzero identifier. HTTP/2 limits the increment and the resulting window to 2^31-1 bytes, or 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF). This report calls that maximum MAX.

The client can also send a SETTINGS frame containing a SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE parameter. This changes the starting credit for new streams. nginx must also adjust each active stream's remaining credit by the difference between the old and new setting values. It does not change the connection's credit. A reduction can therefore leave an active stream with negative credit until the client grants more. The connection window has no equivalent reduction: it must remain between zero and MAX. RFC 9113, section 6.9 defines these limits and the required errors.

nginx stores the connection counter in h2c->send_window, where h2c is the HTTP/2 connection record. Its size_t type is an unsigned integer: on the verified 64-bit build it can hold values from zero to 2^64-1. The size_t type can therefore hold values above HTTP/2's maximum connection window of 2^31-1 bytes (MAX). nginx must enforce that protocol limit in its own logic.

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.h
#define NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW ((1U << 31) - 1) // <--- [1]
struct ngx_http_v2_connection_s {
    // ...
    size_t send_window;                         // <--- [2]
    // ...
};
struct ngx_http_v2_stream_s {
    // ...
    ssize_t send_window;
    // ...
};

The rule that the connection counter at [2] must never exceed MAX at [1] is the connection-window invariant. The separate stream counter, stream->send_window, is explicitly declared as ssize_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. That allows SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE to make a stream's credit temporarily negative. The connection counter remains unsigned. The later unsafe conversion occurs when the output filter treats excessive connection credit as a signed 64-bit off_t response length.

Leveraging vulnerability has four main stages:

  1. By slowing its reading of server output, the client keeps selected DATA frames queued and unstarted. It raises the connection's credit to MAX and the selected streams' credit to just below MAX. A SETTINGS frame that increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough to exceed the stream limit makes nginx close those streams while leaving the connection usable. Request cleanup then restores the reserved credit above MAX.

  2. An unsigned subtraction in the next connection WINDOW_UPDATE check underflows. Repeated accepted WINDOW_UPDATE frames can then raise the counter into the upper half of its 64-bit range without requiring the addition to wrap.

  3. On the verified 64-bit build, nginx interprets that excessive counter as a negative response length and creates an invalid buffer. Buffered TLS output then passes a huge unsigned byte count to the memory-copy function memcpy, causing out-of-bounds reads and writes.

  4. These constrained memory accesses depend on the build and selected copy routine. With a suitable memory layout, an attacker can use disclosed addresses and controlled overwrites to execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Cancelling queued DATA restores too much credit

When nginx queues a DATA frame at [3], it subtracts the frame's DATA length from the connection's credit counter at [4] and then from the stream's credit counter. This reserves the credit before the bytes reach the client and prevents other streams from spending the same connection credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
ngx_http_v2_queue_frame(h2c, frame);       // <--- [3]

h2c->send_window -= frame_size;            // <--- [4]
stream->send_window -= frame_size;
stream->queued++;

An attacker can keep a later response queued by slowing or stopping its reading of earlier server output. Once the transport cannot accept more output, nginx must wait. This condition is transport backpressure. The attacker needs enough of it to keep the selected DATA frame unstarted: none of that frame's bytes have yet entered TLS output or the socket. Stopping response reads does not prevent the client from sending control frames in the other direction.

While the DATA remains queued, the client sends a connection WINDOW_UPDATE that raises nginx's reduced counter to MAX. The problem appears when the request that owns the queued DATA then closes. Its request-cleanup handler removes the unstarted DATA and returns the reserved credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup()
// ...
for ( ;; ) {
    frame = *fn;
    if (frame == NULL) {
        break;
    }
    if (frame->stream == stream && !frame->blocked) { // <--- [5]
        *fn = frame->next;
        window += frame->length;                      // <--- [6]
        if (--stream->queued == 0) {
            break;
        }
        continue;
    }
    fn = &frame->next;
}
// ...
h2c->send_window += window;                           // <--- [7]

The test at [5] selects removable, unstarted frames for that request. The local variable window totals their DATA lengths at [6]. The addition at [7] does not check whether restoring those bytes takes the connection counter above MAX.

For example, restoring 1,393 bytes after the counter has reached 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF) produces 2,147,485,040 (0x80000570). This value is invalid under HTTP/2 as it exceeds MAX, although it still fits in a 64-bit size_t; the addition has not yet wrapped around. The unchecked restoration at [7] is the first invalid state in the vulnerability. The attacker still needs a way to close the selected requests while preserving the connection, so the excessive counter can be used again.

A SETTINGS error closes the stream but leaves the connection usable

When a SETTINGS frame increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough that an active stream's credit would exceed MAX, nginx terminates that stream but leaves the HTTP/2 connection usable. A client can create this condition by first sending a stream WINDOW_UPDATE to put the selected stream just below MAX. It then sends a SETTINGS frame that increases the initial stream-window setting. For example, changing the setting from 65,535 to 65,537 adds two bytes to every active stream. A stream already at MAX-1 would become MAX+1, even though the new setting value itself is allowed.

RFC 9113 requires this condition to end the connection with FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR. nginx instead calls ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream() for each affected stream. That function sends RST_STREAM, which ends an individual stream, and causes the request to be cleaned up. The loop then continues using the same connection:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c
// ngx_http_v2_adjust_windows()
// ...
if (delta > 0
    && stream->send_window
          > (ssize_t) (NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - delta))
{
    if (ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream(h2c, stream,
                                     NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR)
        == NGX_ERROR)
    {
        return NGX_ERROR;
    }
    continue;                                      // <--- [8]
}

Here, delta is the difference between the new and old setting values. Request cleanup performs [5] through [7], while continue at [8] leaves the HTTP/2 connection open. The attacker can now send further frames on the connection whose credit has exceeded MAX.

When another connection WINDOW_UPDATE arrives, nginx tries to calculate how much additional credit is still allowed:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c
// ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()
// ...
if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { // <--- [9]
    // ...
    return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c,
                                        NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR);
}
h2c->send_window += window;                            // <--- [10]

In this function, window is the increment received from the client. The subtraction at [9] is safe only while the stored counter is no greater than MAX. If cleanup has restored R excess bytes, the intended allowance is MAX - (MAX + R), or -R. Unsigned arithmetic cannot represent that negative result. On the verified 64-bit build it wraps to 2^64 - R, a very large positive number. This is the integer underflow identified by CWE-191.

The incorrect allowance lets further client increments pass the check. By sending many increments, each no greater than MAX, the client can raise the counter to 2^63 or above without wrapping the addition itself, shown at [10] above. Such a value has the top bit of its 64-bit representation set. It is still an unsigned value, but it no longer fits in a signed 64-bit integer. That distinction matters when nginx prepares the next response.

This amplification accounts for the large traffic requirement. A connection WINDOW_UPDATE occupies 13 HTTP/2 bytes: a nine-byte frame header and a four-byte payload. The credit granted by that frame is not data actually transmitted. Reaching the near-2^64 values used for the confirmed read/write path takes about 2^33 increments, or 104 GiB. nginx also limits control-frame traffic relative to other received data. The current code-execution reproduction sends about 15 GiB of additional request-header traffic to stay within that limit, bringing its reported plaintext total to about 119.02 GiB. An in-memory nginx buffer is described by a ngx_buf_t record. Its pos pointer is the memory address of the next byte to send. Its last pointer is the address immediately after the available data. // src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c
// ngx_http_v2_send_chain()
// ...
if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) {
    limit = h2c->send_window;                         // <--- [11]
}
if (limit > stream->send_window) {
    limit = (stream->send_window > 0) ? stream->send_window : 0;
}
// ...
if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) {
    frame_size = (size_t) limit;                      // <--- [12]
}
// ...

while ((off_t) rest >= size) {                        // <--- [13]
    // ...
}
if (rest) {
    cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf,
                                       offset, rest); // <--- [14]
    // ...
}

Casting the same value back to off_t makes it negative again, so [13] skips the loop that would normally consume and bound the available body bytes. // ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow()
static ngx_chain_t *

    off_t offset, off_t size)
{
    // ...
    ngx_memcpy(chunk, buf, sizeof(ngx_buf_t));
    // ...
    if (ngx_buf_in_memory(chunk)) {

One route enters this backward-copy branch when D and Q are different and the unsigned difference D-Q is smaller than n. This includes the ordinary case where D is above Q and n is close to the unsigned 64-bit maximum.

// glibc 2.41: sysdeps/x86_64/multiarch/memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S
// Function: CPU-selected memcpy implementation, backward-copy branch
    // ...
L(more_8x_vec_backward):
    // ...
    leaq (VEC_SIZE * -4 + -1)(%rdi, %rdx), %rcx // <--- [20]
    // ...
    andq $-(VEC_SIZE), %rcx                     // <--- [21]
    // ...
L(loop_4x_vec_backward):
    // ... load and store four 32-byte vectors
    addq $(VEC_SIZE * -4), %rcx                 // <--- [22]
    cmpq %rcx, %rdi                             // <--- [23]
    jb L(loop_4x_vec_backward)
    // ... store the previously loaded leading and trailing vectors
    VZEROUPPER_RETURN                           // <--- [24]

The full glibc assembly source shows the omitted loads and stores. At [20], leaq calculates an address without reading memory. Its 64-bit result keeps only the low 64 bits. At [21], andq rounds that address down to a 32-byte boundary. Calling the resulting destination address cursor, the calculation is:

cursor = align_down_32((D + n - 129) modulo 2^64)
       = align_down_32(D - d - 129), when n = 2^64-d

Here, align_down_32 means rounding down to the nearest address divisible by 32; it is explanatory notation, not a glibc function. For an ordinary heap address and a small d, the calculated cursor is already below D.

The loop starts by copying one 128-byte block. Instruction [22] then moves the cursor backward by another 128 bytes. The comparison and unsigned jump at [23] repeat the loop only while D < cursor. Because the cursor is already below D, the jump is not taken. The routine writes its remaining leading and trailing vectors, then returns at [24]. It has not copied the enormous requested range: the wrapped address has made the loop stop after a small set of accesses. Those accesses can still read and overwrite memory outside the actual buffers.

items.title: CVE-2026-114938: Reported Critical Pre-authentication Remote Code Execution in Java 17
items.summary:
Overview

On November 17, 2026, Oracle released patches for CVE-2026-114938, a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) in the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder used by OpenJDK and its downstream distributions, such as Oracle Java SE, and Oracle GraalVM. The vulnerability, dubbed “Java4Shell” by finders Calif, can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash a Java application or execute code with the privileges of its Java process. Oracle rates the vulnerability High, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 and high attack complexity, in its November security advisory.

Affected OpenJDK runtimes enable the vulnerable Base64 optimization by default when the Java virtual machine (JVM) can use the required x86-64 CPU features, including AVX-512 VBMI. A Java application exposes the flaw when it passes untrusted data to that optimized decoder. For example, a web service may decode HTTP Basic credentials before it checks the username and password. Red Hat reports no known exposure on ARM64 or on x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI in its OpenJDK bulletin.

Calif’s disclosure states that they demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against several popular Java based applications, and they have published a local proof of concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-114938, which can test if a local JDK is vulnerable.

Given the ubiquitous nature of Java and its deployment across enterprise environments, Rapid7 recommends identifying and remediating affected systems, with a focus on Internet exposed systems, on an emergency basis and outside of normal patching cycles.

Rapid7 is actively monitoring the situation and will update this blog as new information arrives.

For the latest vendor release information, refer to Oracle's November security update notice and OpenJDK's vulnerability advisories.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-114938 affects a hardware-specific optimization in HotSpot, the Java virtual machine used by many OpenJDK distributions. When frequently used Base64 decoding code is compiled, HotSpot can substitute a native routine that processes multiple bytes at once. The vulnerable path requires an x86-64 runtime, CPU features including AVX-512 VBMI, and effective JVM settings that permit the optimizing compiler and Base64 intrinsic. Consequently, an affected Java version alone does not establish that a particular application is exploitable.

The defect occurs when that routine processes a malformed final Base64 group. Its calculation of the remaining output length can become negative, enabling a wider memory write than the destination can accommodate. Confirmed malformed-tail cases produce a 64-byte store extending 62 or 63 bytes beyond the calculated decoded-output length. Java subsequently rejects the malformed input, but catching that exception does not undo the corruption. Damage to another object can remain unnoticed until later activity, including garbage collection, crashes the JVM.

Turning this constrained overwrite into code execution requires additional work. A reliable exploit typically needs to influence which objects occupy the affected memory, convert the initial corruption into useful access to other objects, and identify application or runtime behavior that permits further execution. The practical outcome therefore depends on the application, JVM build, memory layout, and security boundaries. This distinction explains why a working corruption trigger does not establish a portable exploit for every Java service.

Remote exposure arises when an application passes attacker-controlled data to the affected decoder. Authentication headers and tokens are relevant examples, but reachability must be established for the actual implementation. The published OpenJDK fix hands final groups shorter than four bytes to the ordinary Java decoder. Organizations should apply their runtime vendor's fixed build and restart affected JVMs; disabling Base64 intrinsics with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics is a temporary mitigation where supported.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 recommends applying the November security update as soon as possible, starting with internet-facing services that decode credentials or tokens before authentication. Identify the runtime vendor and full build each service uses, including Java runtimes bundled with applications, appliances, and container images.

OpenJDK lists release versions 17, 21, 25, and 27 as affected by CVE-2026-114938 in its November 17 advisory. Red Hat identifies OpenJDK 17.0.6 as the earliest affected version 17.

Oracle separately identifies its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack as affected in the Java risk matrix. The table below pairs affected Oracle builds with the November updates listed in the JDK security baselines, Enterprise Performance Pack release notes, and GraalVM release calendar.

Vulnerable Java Version

Patched Version (Official Release Notes)

Oracle Java SE 8 Performance Edition

8u511b33-perf

8u513-perf

Oracle Java SE 17

17.0.21.0.3

17.0.21.1

Oracle Java SE 21

21.0.13.0.3

21.0.13.1

Oracle Java SE 25

25.0.5.0.3

25.0.5.1

Oracle Java SE 27

27.0.1.0.3

27.0.1.1

Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17

17.0.21.0.3

17.0.21.1

Oracle GraalVM for JDK 21

21.0.13.0.3

21.0.13.1

Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition

21.3.20.0.3

21.3.20.1

For other OpenJDK based distributions, use the patched package from your Java vendor. If an application or appliance bundles Java, use the product vendor’s update. Rebuild affected container images, redeploy the workloads, and restart affected services. Verify that each running Java process uses the patched build, as CIRCL recommends.

If you cannot patch an affected OpenJDK service immediately, restart its JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. This disables hardware acceleration for Base64 decoding while leaving other CPU optimizations in place.

To learn how to use Rapid7 capabilities to find systems affected by this vulnerability and for answers to common questions, read the Oracle OpenJDK Java (CVE-2026-114938) documentation.

items.title: Who Has Access to Claude? Bring AI Identity and Access Context Into Surface Command
items.summary:
Approving an AI service is only the starting point. As employees adopt Claude and their responsibilities change, security teams need to know who has access, which users hold administrative privileges, and whether those roles and group memberships still reflect the work they do.

IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that, among studied organizations reporting an AI-related breach, 97% lacked proper AI access controls. The finding highlights a broader challenge: AI adoption needs security practices that extend beyond the initial approval, supported by information teams can use to review access with administrators and service owners.

Rapid7 Surface Command now integrates with Claude’s Compliance API, bringing supported organization, user, role, group, and settings information into the same platform teams use to understand other assets and identities. The integration helps security teams make enterprise Claude access part of their existing review practices.

Bring enterprise AI access into your security view

An account list tells security teams who is present, while roles and group memberships help explain how access is organized and where further review may be needed. Surface Command’s integration with Claude’s Compliance API brings together:

  • Organizations and users: Visibility into the Claude organization and its associated user accounts.

  • Roles and groups: Context to understand users’ assigned roles and group memberships.

  • Organizational settings: Available configuration information to support review of the enterprise Claude environment.

With those details in Surface Command, practitioners can examine Claude identities alongside the other assets and identities they manage. That gives them a clearer basis for working with service owners to evaluate whether access remains appropriate as teams and responsibilities change.

The integration focuses on administrative visibility. It does not ingest Claude conversation content, provide threat detection on Claude activity, or control Claude’s behavior.

From a user record to an informed access review

Consider a security practitioner reviewing administrative access to Claude. In Surface Command, they can inspect an imported user’s details, review their organization role and administrative status, and examine their group memberships. The relationship graph provides a visual view of how that user connects to the organization and its groups, making those associations easier to follow.

The practitioner can then work with the service owner to confirm whether administrative privileges are still needed, whether group memberships reflect current responsibilities, and whether those assignments align with the organization’s access model.

Surface Command provides information to support the review, while the team applies its policies and judgment to determine whether a change is needed.

Support AI adoption with clearer accountability

As Claude becomes part of everyday work, reviewing its users and access relationships becomes part of managing the environment. Bringing that information into Surface Command helps security practitioners and service owners work from a shared understanding of assigned roles and group memberships. It supports more informed access decisions and helps security leaders incorporate enterprise AI into established oversight practices.

Get started with Claude and Surface Command today

The integration is available through the Anthropic connector in the Rapid7 Extension Library. Using Claude’s Compliance API requires a Compliance API key and the appropriate entitlement for your Claude organization.

Visit the connector page to get started and see how Surface Command brings Claude users, roles, and group relationships into view.

items.title: Rapid7 Detected Exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center, N-able N-central also Exploited
items.summary:
Overview

On November 6, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-90436, a critical unsafe reflection vulnerability (CWE-470) in Axis 1.x that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Apache Axis is a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) implementation used for the creation of Java Web services. CISA has assigned CVE-2026-90436 a CVSS score of 9.8 Critical.

Since the initial November 6 disclosure, it has transpired that some versions of Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central use the affected Axis library and are vulnerable to CVE-2026-90436. Both products require a non-default configuration in order to be vulnerable.

CVE-2026-90436 is now being actively exploited in the wild against both known affected products. On November 13, 2026, Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment. Separately, on November 13, 2026, N-able reported exploitation in the wild against N-central for a vulnerability that strongly correlates to CVE-2026-90436. A proof-of-concept exploit that leverages CVE-2026-90436 and targets N-central was published on November 12, 2026, as part of a series of public zero-day disclosures against N-central.

Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles.

MDR observed exploitation

On November 13, 2026, Rapid7's MDR team responded to a surge of alerts firing on the abnormal child processes launched by an Atlassian Confluence server. A review of the Confluence access logs revealed unauthenticated POST requests to /plugins/servlet/soap-axis1/confluenceservice-v2, each returning an HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error). Despite the error responses, endpoint telemetry showed Confluence's Java process launching Bash and curl as the dedicated confluence service account, within seconds of these requests. The attacker proceeded to run hundreds of hex-encoded shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains. Each command wrapped its output in labeled delimiters, and carried sequential task IDs, a structure that suggests the use of AI-assisted automated tooling.

From this foothold, the attacker enumerated the host, network, Confluence configuration, encryption keys, and database settings. Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys. The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives.

The attacker continued extensive enumeration, mapping various internal services. They used a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, then ran Impacket's GetNPUsers.py against a domain controller, attempting an AS-REP roasting attack.

Although these attempts failed, the access we did observe relied on credentials stored in Confluence, and roughly four hours after the first exploit request, the attacker had acquired a service account credential and began querying a production cloud data warehouse. Approximately twelve hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from 192.238.253[.]176. The same address appeared in the hostname of the Pinggy tunnel and in exploit requests observed earlier in the intrusion.

Mitigation guidance

Prioritize internet-accessible instances with the relevant APIs enabled, and check internal deployments as well. Apply the product-specific actions below, then investigate systems that were exposed for evidence of compromise.

Axis 1.x through 1.4 is affected but has reached end of life (EOL) and Apache does not plan to publish a fixed Axis 1.x release. Apache recommends moving to another SOAP engine (for example, Apache Axis 2) or using an Axis 1.x build with this patch applied. Organizations using products that are affected by this issue should follow the product vendor's specific remediation instructions.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

Atlassian lists versions 1.x through to 9.x as affected when “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)” is enabled. Version 9.2.28 is the fixed release. The setting has been off by default for new installations since version 3.0. Confluence version 10.x and later removed the feature so are not vulnerable, and Atlassian Cloud is unaffected.

Affected users should upgrade to version 9.2.28 or a current unaffected 10.x release. If patching must wait, an administrator can open “General Configuration” and “Further Configuration”, edit the settings, clear “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)”, and save. The change takes effect without restarting Confluence, but integrations using the API may stop working.

Follow the Confluence advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions.

N-able N-central

On-premises administrators should confirm that “Legacy API” is disabled, even on 2026.4 HF2. N-able states that it is off by default, and provides instructions for disabling Legacy API. Its November 13 guidance says hosted environments received temporary protections directly; customers in both hosting models must still follow the vendor's Agent and Probe upgrade guidance. N-able also temporarily disabled the Intune integration as a precaution. Refer to the N-able security update for these responsibilities.

Update: On November 16, 2026, N-able released N-central 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) which addresses multiple issues including seventeen new CVEs. The “Legacy API” feature which exposed the vulnerable CVE-2026-90436 Axis attack surface has been disabled in this new release. N-central users should upgrade to N-central 2026.4 HF3 on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles.

Follow the N-able advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions.

IOCs

The presence of these IOCs in logs should prompt investigation, but the absence of these addresses does not confirm that an environment was unaffected.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

The following IP addresses and domains are associated with observed exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center:

  • 192.238.253[.]176

  • 5.133.47[.]243

  • 163.182.68[.]109

  • 104.13.106[.]166

  • *.trycloudflare[.]com

  • wpefh-192-238-253-176.free.pinggy[.]net

  • webhook[.]site

N-able N-central

N-able's November 13 incident update lists these IP addresses as IOCs for N-central customers who had not disabled Legacy API.

  • 157.20.241[.]16

  • 139.99.69[.]109

  • 79.76.51[.]56

The vendor's update also lists associated URLs for use in compromise assessment.

Updates

  • November 16, 2026: Initial publication.

  • November 17, 2026: Updated Remediation section for N-central.
  • November 17, 2026: Added the MDR observed exploitation section and updated IOCs.
